    RC lab with an AC source: walkthrough

    In this lab you measure the time constant of an RC circuit by watching a capacitor charge and discharge on an oscilloscope. This walkthrough is a rehearsal: you get a virtual resistor, capacitor, function generator and oscilloscope that behave like the real ones on the bench, so that in the lab you already know what to do and what to expect.

    How it works

    • The walkthrough follows the lab handout: Part A (calculations), Part B (circuit and display), Part C (cursor measurements).
    • There are 9 checkpoints worth 5 points each, 45 points in total, with unlimited attempts. The next section opens once the current checkpoint is solved.
    • Your virtual components have their own slightly imperfect values, like real ones. Your numbers differ from your classmates’.
    • The values you find are collected in an answer sheet at the end, which you can print.
    • Everything works with a keyboard, and every oscilloscope screen also has a text description.

    Equipment and self-calibration

    Equipment needed
    ItemWhat it does in this lab
    One \(1.0\ \text{k}\Omega\) resistorLimits the charging current; together with \(C\) it sets the time constant.
    One \(1.0\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitorCharges and discharges; its voltage is what you watch.
    One function generatorThe AC source. Set to a square wave, it alternates between two constant voltages.
    One oscilloscope (RIGOL DS1102E)Plots voltage against time on two channels and measures them with cursors.
    One breadboard with jumper wiresHolds the circuit without soldering.
    One BNC to alligator cableBrings the generator’s output to the breadboard: red clip to the signal, black clip to ground.
    Two oscilloscope probesChannel 1 watches the generator; channel 2 watches the capacitor. Set both to X1.
    One multimeterMeasures the actual resistance and capacitance before you build the circuit.

    Reminder: self-calibration

    If the oscilloscope shows values much larger than the few volts you expect for the peak-to-peak voltage, run the self-calibration:

    1. Disconnect everything from the oscilloscope.
    2. Press the Utility button.
    3. Scroll down twice by pressing the down arrow.
    4. Select the Self-Cal option and follow the on-screen instructions.
    5. Be patient: this may take a few minutes.

    The physics: charging a capacitor

    When a constant voltage \(V_{\max}\) is applied to a resistor and an uncharged capacitor in series, the capacitor voltage rises as

    \[V_C(t)=V_{\max}\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right),\qquad \tau=RC\]

    Two numbers to remember

    1. One time constant. At \(t=\tau\): \(V_C=V_{\max}(1-e^{-1})=V_{\max}(1-0.368)=0.632\,V_{\max}\). So \(\tau\) is the time for the capacitor to reach 63.2% of its final voltage. This is what you will measure.
    2. Fully charged. At \(t=5\tau\): \(V_C=V_{\max}(1-e^{-5})=0.993\,V_{\max}\). After about \(5\tau\) the capacitor is, for all practical purposes, fully charged.
    3. Units check. \(\Omega\cdot\text{F}=\dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{A}}\cdot\dfrac{\text{C}}{\text{V}}=\dfrac{\text{C}}{\text{C/s}}=\text{s}\). With \(1\ \text{k}\Omega\) and \(1\ \mu\text{F}\), \(\tau=10^3\times10^{-6}\ \text{s}=1\ \text{ms}\).

    Why a square wave, and at what frequency?

    A square wave holds a constant voltage for half a cycle, then switches for the other half. During the first half the capacitor charges; during the second half it discharges. To see a complete charge and a complete discharge, each half cycle must last about \(5\tau\):

    \[T_{\text{cycle}}=10\tau,\qquad f_{\text{nominal}}=\frac{1}{T_{\text{cycle}}}=\frac{1}{10\tau}\]

    On the bench the generator usually swings symmetrically, for example from \(-5\ \text{V}\) to \(+5\ \text{V}\) rather than from 0 to 10 V. Nothing changes: the capacitor still moves exponentially from one level toward the other, and \(V_{\max}\) is the full height of that swing.

    Part A: calculate the time constant and nominal frequency

    Components are never exactly their labeled value; tolerances of 5% to 10% are common for capacitors. That is why you measure them first.

    1. Use the multimeter to measure the resistance \(R\) of the resistor and the capacitance \(C\) of the capacitor. Measure each component out of the circuit, on the resistance (\(\Omega\)) and capacitance settings.
    2. Enter those values in the answer sheet.
    3. Calculate \(\tau_{\text{calculated}}=RC\) from the measured values.
    4. Calculate the nominal frequency \(f_{\text{nominal}}=1/T_{\text{cycle}}=1/(10\tau)\).

    Part B: building the circuit

    The circuit is a series RC loop driven by the function generator. Channel 1 watches the generator’s output; channel 2 watches the capacitor.

    1. Set up the circuit on the breadboard as shown in the photo: resistor from the positive rail to a free row, capacitor from that row to the negative rail.
    2. Connect the function generator to the rails with the BNC to alligator cable: red clip to the positive rail, black clip to the negative rail. Turn it on, set it to a square wave at \(f_{\text{nominal}}\), and set the amplitude to mid-range; you will adjust it later.
    3. Connect the probes: channel 1 tip to the positive rail (the generator), channel 1 ground clip to the negative rail, channel 2 tip to the row joining the resistor and the capacitor. The channel 2 ground clip stays unconnected. Set both probes to X1.

    Checkpoint 2: where does channel 2 go?

    Part B: setting up the display

    Here is a virtual version of your bench, wired as in the photos. Follow the handout steps:

    1. Turn the oscilloscope on (done for you).
    2. Press AUTO. If the capacitor voltage barely reaches its maximum before the square wave switches, the frequency is too high: lower it on the generator.
    3. Press Measure, then Display All, and check that the peak-to-peak voltage of channel 1 is about \(10.0\ \text{V}\). Adjust it with the AMPL dial if needed.
    4. Select a channel and use the vertical and horizontal position controls to put the patterns on top of each other; use the scale controls to resize them.
    5. Once the pattern is well adjusted, turn channel 1 off; you won’t need it in Part C.
    6. Record the actual frequency of the generator, \(f_{\text{actual}}\).
    Photos of the real oscilloscope for these steps

    Checkpoint 5: what does this screen tell you?

    Part C: measuring the time constant with cursors

    Channel 1 is off and the screen is zoomed on one charge and discharge of the capacitor. You will measure in three stages, each with its own checkpoint below the oscilloscope.

    1. Press Cursor and set Mode: Manual, Type: Y, Source: CH2.
    2. Select cursor A (white line). Move it to the top of the voltage displayed.
    3. Select cursor B (yellow line). Move it to the bottom of the voltage displayed.
    4. Read \(\Delta Y\): this is \(V_{\max}\) for the capacitor. Checkpoint 6.
    5. Calculate \(V_\tau=0.632\times V_{\max}\). Checkpoint 7.
    6. Select cursor A again and move it down until \(\Delta Y=V_\tau\). The A line now marks the 63.2% level.
    7. Optional: use the horizontal position to put the point where the trace crosses that level on a major grid line.
    8. Change the cursor Type to X. Move cursor A to where the voltage starts to rise; move cursor B to where the trace crosses the \(V_\tau\) level.
    9. Read \(\Delta X\): this is \(\tau_{\text{measured}}\). Checkpoint 8.

    These are the values you found in the walkthrough. In the real lab you will fill in the same quantities with your own bench measurements, and they will differ a little from these.

    Before you go to the lab

    • Measure \(R\) and \(C\) with the multimeter before building the circuit.
    • Probes on X1. Only one probe ground clip connected, on the generator’s ground side.
    • If the readings look far too large, run Self-Cal (Utility, down twice, Self-Cal).
    • Frequency too high? The capacitor never flattens out. Lower the frequency.
    • Expect \(\tau_{\text{measured}}\) within a few percent of \(RC\). Ask yourself where a larger difference could come from.
